title: Found 3-5% arbitrage spreads in prediction markets consistently. Is it real edge?
author: YukiChuuu
selftext:
Been scanning Polymarket vs Kalshi and there are still consistent arb opportunities sitting in plain sight. I’m regularly seeing the same events priced differently across platforms, with spreads of around 4–6 cents after fees and many of them lasting \~1 hour.

The inefficiency comes down to fragmentation — most traders only stick to one platform, so the gaps just sit there. Thinner liquidity on certain events makes it even better, though position limits can be restrictive, and running accounts across multiple platforms means dealing with KYC and funding friction on each one.

I built synpath to aggregate real-time data and match same markets across platforms for exactly this. It's open-source if anyone wants to run their own scans: [https://github.com/Synpath-ai/synpath](https://github.com/Synpath-ai/synpath)

Anyone else trading prediction market arb? What kind of slippage and fill rates are you seeing on smaller events?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Possibly, but "same event, different price" and "free money" aren't the same thing. The first thing I'd check is the resolution criteria on both sides. Different sources, cutoff times, or edge-case rules (what happens if a print is revised, a date slips, or the wording is ambiguous) can make two contracts that look identical price differently for good reason. A lot of apparent arbs are really the market pricing that resolution risk.

Then there's capital lock-up. A 5-cent net spread on a contract that resolves in three months is a very different annualized return than one that resolves next week, and your capital is stuck on both platforms until then. Compare it to what T-bills pay on the same cash. Also consider leg risk (one side fills and the other doesn't, especially on thin books), depth at the price you saw, USDC versus USD conversion and withdrawal costs, and platform or account risk.

Spreads that last an hour on thin markets are also a hint that others are seeing the same thing and finding it not worth it, so I'd want to know the realized numbers: fill rates on both legs, average size, and net annualized return after all costs.

For markets tied to scheduled releases like CPI, Fed decisions, or earnings, mismatched resolution sources and timing are the usual culprit. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing that could help check whether two contracts really resolve on the same data point.

Do you have realized P&L from actually running it, or is it mostly scanned spreads so far?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Some of it is real, but most of those gaps are paying you for risks that don't show up in the spread.

The big one is resolution wording. Two markets that look like the same event often aren't: different sources, different cutoff times, different handling of edge cases like a delayed announcement or a recount. When they diverge you aren't hedged at all, you hold two opposite bets that can both lose. Read both rule texts line by line before calling anything an arb.

Second is capital lockup. 4 cents on a market that resolves in five months is a thin annualized return once you count the money sitting on two platforms, plus deposit and withdrawal friction on each.

Third is legging. If one side fills and the book on the other moves before you get there, you're holding a naked position on a thin market.

The gaps that last an hour usually last because of one of those three, not because nobody noticed.
